COURT OF QUEBEC

Division"

PRESIDING:

THE HONOURABLE

CLAUDE LEBLOND J.C.Q.

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN

Prosecutrix

v.

SAÏD NAMOUH

Accused

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The accused stood trial on the following
charges:

1-

Conspiracy to use explosives

Between
April and September 2007, Saïd Namouh, a.k.a. Saïd Mamouh, a.k.a. Ashraf, at
Maskinongé and Trois-Rivières, District of Trois-Rivières, at Montréal,
District of Montreal, and elsewhere in the Province of Quebec, and at Vienna,
Austria,
did conspire with Mohammed Mahmoud and other persons as yet
unknown
, with the purpose of committing an indictable offence, to wit:
deliver, place, discharge or detonate an explosive or other lethal device to,
into, in or against a place of public use with intent to cause death or serious
bodily injury or with intent to cause extensive destruction of such a place,
thereby committing the offence set out in
s. 465(1)
(
c
) of the
Criminal
Code
, referring to s. 431.2(2) of the said
Code
.

2-

Participation  in the activity of a terrorist group

Between November 2006 and September 2007, Saïd Namouh, a.k.a. Saïd
Mamouh, a.k.a. Ashraf, at Maskinongé and Trois-Rivières, District of
Trois-Rivières, at Montréal, District of Montreal, and elsewhere in the
Province of Quebec, in Austria and in Germany, did
knowingly participate
in or contribute to, directly or indirectly, an activity of a terrorist group

for the purpose of enhancing the ability of any terrorist group to facilitate
or carry out a terrorist activity, thereby committing the offence set out in s.
82.18 of the
Criminal Code
.

3-

Facilitating terrorist activity

Between November 2006 and September 2007, Saïd Namouh, a.k.a. Saïd
Mamouh a.k.a. Ashraf, at Maskinongé and Trois-Rivières, District of
Trois-Rivières, at Montreal, District of Montreal and elsewhere in the Province
of Quebec, in Austria and in Germany,
did knowingly facilitate a
terrorist activity
, thereby committing the offence set out in
s. 83.19

of the
Criminal Code
.

4-
Extortion in association with a
terrorist group

Between November
2006 and September 2007, Saïd Namouh, a.k.a. Saïd Mamouh, a.k.a. Ashraf, at
Maskinongé and Trois-Rivières, District of Trois-Rivières, at Montreal,
District of Montreal and elsewhere in the Province of Quebec, in Austria and in
Germany,
did commit an indictable offence, to wit: extortion, for the
benefit of or under the instructions of a terrorist group or in association
with a terrorist group
, thereby committing an indictable offence set
out in
s. 83.2
of the
Criminal Code
in reference to
s. 346
of the
Criminal
Code
.

[
2
]

The Court will begin with counts 2, 3, and 4,
since the facts in those charges are relevant to the analysis of the first
count.

Counts 2 and 3: Participation in
the activities of a terrorist group and facilitation of terrorist activity

[
3
]

Admissions were made by the defence at trial.
The issues were further clarified through additional admissions made during
oral argument by the defence.

[
4
]

The defence wondered whether it had been proved
beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused participated in the creation and
distribution of various videos circulated on the Internet by the GIMF that had
been filed as evidence.

[
5
]

Later on in its oral argument, the defence
admitted the involvement of the accused. Consequently, the only remaining issue
in dispute is whether this participation was tantamount to participation in the
activities of a terrorist group and facilitation of a terrorist activity.

The
defence posited that the issue was whether the accused actively encouraged
these activities.

[
6
]

Later on during oral argument, the defence
admitted that
if
the GIMF was a terrorist group within the
meaning of s. 83.01
Cr. C
., the only possible conclusion was that he had
participated in the activities of a terrorist group and facilitated terrorist
activities.

[
7
]

There was, however, the question of the
intention of the accused, that is, whether the accused had participated in the
activities of a terrorist group with the intention of enhancing its ability
within the meaning of s. 83.18
Cr. C
.

[
8
]

The accused participated in the creation and
distribution of videos through the GIMF. The purpose of the videos was, at a
minimum, to increase the group’s knowledge about terrorism. Consequently, the
purpose of the participation of the accused could only have been to enhance the
ability of the group to carry out a terrorist activity or to facilitate it.

[
9
]

The defence has no argument to counter this
logic. It is also unable to identify any other intention that the accused could
have had in his admitted participation.

[
10
]

That is why the Court finds that the only issue
in dispute regarding counts 2 and 3 is whether the GIMF is a terrorist group
within the meaning of the Act.

Is the GIMF a terrorist group?

[
11
]

Section 83.01(1)(
b
)
Cr. C
. reads
as follows:

“terrorist activity” means

(b) an act or omission, in or
outside Canada:

(i) that is committed

(A) in whole or in part for a
political, religious or ideological purpose, objective or cause, and (B) in
whole or in part with the intention of intimidating the public, or a segment of
the public, with regard to its security, or compelling a person, a government
or a domestic or an international organization to do or to refrain from doing
any act, whether the public or the person, government or organization is inside
or outside Canada, and

(ii) that intentionally:

(A) causes death or serious bodily
harm to a person by the use of violence,

(B) endangers a person’s life,

(C) causes a serious risk to the
health or safety of the public or any segment of the public,

(D) causes substantial property
damage, whether to public or private property, if causing such damage is likely
to result in the conduct or harm referred to in any of clauses (A) to (C),

(E) causes serious interference
with or serious disruption of an essential service, facility or system, whether
public or private, other than as a result of advocacy, protest, dissent or
stoppage of work that is not intended to result in the conduct or harm referred
to in any of clauses (A) to (C),

and includes a conspiracy, attempt
or
threat
to commit any such act or omission, or being an accessory
after the fact or
counselling
in relation to any such act or omission,
but, for greater certainty, does not include an act or omission that is
committed during an armed conflict and that, at the time and in the place of
its commission, is in accordance with customary international law or
conventional international law applicable to the conflict, or the activities
undertaken by military forces of a state in the exercise of their official
duties, to the extent that those activities are governed by other rules of
international law terrorist group

”terrorist group” means

a
) an entity that has as one of its
purposes or activities facilitating or carrying out any terrorist activity, or

(b
) a listed entity.

The meaning of “
encourager
” in
the French version of the definition of “terrorist activity” in s. 83.01
Cr.
C
.

[
12
]

The word “
encouragement
” in the French
version of this provision is translated in the English version as
“counselling”. At first glance, the French term appears to be similar to the
definition of the same word in s. 21
Cr. C
., while the English term
appears to be similar to the definition of the word in s. 22
Cr. C
.

[
13
]

In
Ford
, the Court of Appeal for Ontario,

per
MacPherson J.A., considered the difference between these provisions:

[20] ... The Supreme Court of'
Canada has defined "abet" for purposes of party liability as
including "encouraging, instigating, promoting or procuring the crime to
be committed": see
R. v. Greyeyes
(1997),
1997 CanLII 313 (SCC)
, 116 C.C.C. (3d) 334 at
344.
Section 22(3)
of the
Criminal Code
defines "counsel" as
including "procure, solicit or incite". There is no doubt that these
are limited definitions.

[21] However, they are not
identical definitions....

[27] Concerning "aiding"
and "abetting'', the trial judge said:

[T]he
word "aiding'' means help or assist a person. A person can aid a person in
the committing of an offence without being present when the crime is committed.
The second way in which a person can be a party to an offence is by abetting
and the word "abetting" means support or encourage. As with the case
with aiding, a person can be an abettor without being present when a crime is
committed. To be guilty of aiding or abetting there must he some actual
participation or assistance rendered. A person must associate himself with the
criminal venture by participating in it and trying to make if succeed, or
actively encouraging that to occur.

[28] Concerning
"counselling", the trial judge said:

The word "counselling" includes procuring,
soliciting or inciting. I will explain what each of these words means. To
"counsel" means to advise or recommend. To "procure" means
to instigate, encourage or persuade. A person can encourage or persuade without
having instigated the offence. A person "solicits" another when he or
she entreats or urges another to do something. To "incite" has a
similar meaning. It means to urge or stir up or stimulate.

[29] In these passages there is
some overlap in the definitions. The word "encourage" appears in the
definitions or both abetting and counselling. Nevertheless, there is a clear
difference in the definitions. The offence of counselling is limited to oral
encouragement by the accused. However, the activity of abetting requires
"actual participation or assistance rendered''. It may be that the trial
judge's definition of abetting was narrower than the definition enunciated in
R. v. Greyeyes,
supra
. However, that may well have inured to the
appellant's benefit in that he was acquitted of the charge of attempted murder,
the offence grounded in abetting on the facts of this case. In any event, there
was nothing wrong with the trial judge's definition of counselling. Moreover,
his definition of counselling was different than his definition of both aiding
and abetting.
[1]

[
14
]

In
Daoust
, the Supreme Court of Canada
established the rules of interpretation when the French version has a
potentially different meaning from the English:

“26 The
Court has on several occasions discussed how a bilingual statute should be
interpreted in cases where there is a discrepancy between the two versions of
the same text. For example, in
Schreiber v. Canada (Attorney General)
,
[2002] 3 S.C.R. 269,
2002 CSC 62
, at para.
56
, LeBel J. wrote:

A
principle of bilingual statutory interpretation holds that where one version is
ambiguous and the other is clear and unequivocal, the common meaning of the two
versions would
a priori
be preferred; see: Côté,
supra
, at p.
327; and
Tupper v. The Queen
,
1967 CanLII 14 (SCC)
, [1967] S.C.R. 589.  Furthermore,
where one of the two versions is broader than the other, the common meaning
would favour the more restricted or limited meaning: see Côté,
supra
, at
p. 327;
R. v. Dubois
,
1935 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1935] S.C.R. 378;
Maurice

Pollack
Ltée v. Comité paritaire du commerce de détail à Québec
,
1946 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1946] S.C.R.
343;
Pfizer Co. v. Deputy Minister of National Revenue for Customs and
Excise
,
1975 CanLII 194 (SCC)
, [1977] 1 S.C.R. 456, at p. 464‑465; and
Gravel v.
City of St‑Léonard
,
1977 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 660, at p. 669.

As well, in
R. v. Mac
,
[2002] 1 S.C.R. 856,
2002 CSC 24
, at para.5, I stated the following:

The
Criminal
Code
is a bilingual statute of which both the English and French versions
are equally authoritative. In his
Interpretation of Legislation in Canada

(3rd ed. 2000), at p. 327, Pierre‑André Côté reminds us that statutory
interpretation of bilingual enactments begins with a search for the shared
meaning between the two versions.

I would also draw attention to the
two-step analysis proposed by Professor Côté in
The Interpretation of
Legislation in Canada
(3rd ed. 2000), at p. 324, for resolving discordances
resulting from divergences between the two versions of a statute:

. . .
Unless otherwise provided, differences between two official versions of the
same enactment are reconciled by educing the meaning common to both. Should
this prove to be impossible, or if the common meaning seems incompatible with
the intention of the legislature as indicated by the ordinary rules of
interpretation, the meaning arrived at by the ordinary rules should be
retained.

27 There
is, therefore, a specific procedure to be followed when interpreting bilingual
statutes. The first step is to determine whether there is
discordance.  If the two versions are irreconcilable, we must rely on
other principles:  see Côté,
supra
at p. 327. A
purposive and contextual approach is favoured: See, for
example,
Bell ExpressVu Limited Partnership v. Rex
, [2002] 2 S.C.R.
559,
2002 CSC 42
, at para.
26
;
Chieu v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and
Immigration),

[
2002] 1 S.C.R. 84,
2002 CSC 3
, at para.
27
;
R. v.
Sharpe
, [2001] 1 S.C.R. 45,
2001 SCC 2
, at para.
33
.

28 We must
determine whether there is an ambiguity, that is, whether one or both versions
of the statute are “reasonably capable of more than one meaning”:
Bell ExpressVu Ltd
.,
supra
, at para. 29.  If there is an ambiguity in one version but not the other,
the two versions must be reconciled, that is, we must look for the meaning that
is common to both versions:
Côté
,
supra
, at p. 327.  The
common meaning is the version that is plain and not ambiguous: Côté,
supra
,
at p. 327; see
Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. of Canada v. T. Eaton Co
.,

1956 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1956] S.C.R. 610, at p. 614;
Kwiatkowsky V. Minister of Employment and
Immigration
,
1982 CanLII 221 (SCC)
, [1982] 2 S.C.R. 856, at p. 863.

29  If neither version is
ambiguous, or if they both are, the common meaning is normally the narrower
version:
Gravel v. City of St-Léonard
,
1977 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1978] 1 S.C.R. 660, at p. 669;
Pfizer
Co. v. Deputy Minister of National Revenue for Customs and Excise
,
1975 CanLII 194 (SCC)
, [1977] 1
S.C.R. 456, at p. 464-465.  Professor Côté illustrates this point as follows,
at p. 327:

There is
a third possibility: one version may have a broader meaning than another, in
which case the shared meaning is the more narrow of the two.

30 The
second step is to determine whether the common or dominant meaning is,
according to the ordinary rules of statutory interpretation, consistent with
Parliament’s intent: Côté,
supra
, at p.
328-329. At this stage, the words off Lamer J. in
Slaight
Communications Inc. v. Davidson
,
1989 CanLII 92 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1038, at p. 1071, are
instructive:

First of all, therefore, these two versions have to be reconciled if
possible. To do this, an attempt must be made to get from the two versions
of the provision the meaning common to them both and ascertain whether this
appears to be consistent with the purpose and general scheme of the Code.

31 Finally,
it should be borne in mind that some principles of interpretation may only be
applied in cases where there is an ambiguity in an enactment.  As
Iacobucci J. wrote in
Bell ExpressVu
,
supra
, at para. 28: “Other principles of interpretation – such as the strict construction
of penal statutes and the ‘
Charter
values’ presumption – only receive
application where there is ambiguity as to the meaning of a provision”.
[2]

[
15
]

The Honourable Anne McLellan, then Minister of
Justice and Attorney General of Canada, testified before a special Senate
committee on Bill C-36. She stated the following to illustrate the reasons that
Canada needed to enact this bill:

... If terrorists get on the
planes, it is too late. We have failed...

... The approach we have taken in
the bill is a preventive one because punishing terrorists for crimes after they
occur is simply not enough. We must be able to disable organizations before
they put hijackers on planes or threaten our sense of security, as we have seen
in recent days with the scare of anthrax. We cannot wait for terrorists to
strike before we begin investigations and make arrests where there is a
reasonable suspicion that a terrorist act will take place. To wait would be
irresponsible.
[3]

[
16
]

In written argument on the subject, counsel for
the prosecution states:

[
translation
]

60.        We maintain that the
solution that must be retained for a correct interpretation of the difference
between the French and English versions is one that interprets “
encouragement
à la perpetration
” and “counselling” as consistent with the meaning
expressed in
ss. 22
and
464
of the
Criminal Code
;

61.        Our position is
supported by the fact that the contrary interpretation, whereby “
encouragement
à la perpetration
” and “counselling” are interpreted in a manner consistent
with the meaning in
s. 21
of the
Criminal

Code
, would limit the
definition of secondary liability crimes to only those cases where the primary
crime was actually committed;

62.        In actual fact, the
threshold under
s. 21(1)
(
c
) of the
Criminal

Code
with
respect to “abets” requires that the counselling involve “actual participation
or assistance rendered” with respect to a committed crime, as defined in
Ford
,

supra
;

63.        Indeed, it appears to be
impossible to prove “actual participation or assistance rendered” in the
absence of the actual commission of a crime;

64.        Retaining a restrictive
interpretation of “
encouragement à la perpetration
” and “counselling”,
which would attract criminal liability only when the terrorist activity that is
“encouraged” or “counselled” is brought to completion would, in our view, be
entirely contrary to legislative intent.

[
17
]

On this issue, counsel for the defence agrees,
stating that the word “
encouragement
” means active encouragement.

[
18
]

The Court agrees with the prosecution’s argument
that to interpret “
encouragement
” as “actual participation or assistance
rendered” would limit the definition of secondary liability crimes to only
those cases where the primary crime had been committed.

[
19
]

Counsel for the prosecution refers to
Hamilton
,
where the Supreme Court of Canada interpreted the meaning of the word
“counsel”:

29 In short, the
actus reus

for counselling is the
deliberate encouragement or active inducement of the
commission of a criminal offence
.  And the
mens rea
consists in
nothing less than an accompanying
intent
or
conscious disregard of
the substantial and unjustified risk inherent in the counselling
: that is,
it must be shown that the accused either intended that the offence counselled
be committed, or knowingly counselled the commission of the offence while aware
of the unjustified risk that the offence counselled was in fact likely to be
committed as a result of the accused’s conduct.
[4]

[
20
]

This is the meaning the word “counselling” in s.
83.01
Cr. C
. must have in order to be consistent with the French version
while also complying with legislative intent.

[
21
]

In written argument, the prosecution refers to
evidence that, in its view, establishes that the GIMF is a terrorist
group:

[
translation
]

2.2
The GIMF is a terrorist group

The activities alleged against the GIMF that establish that it participates directly in
and, as a subsidiary argument, encourages terrorist activities are:

(a)  compelling a government to do
or to refrain from doing any act and intimidating all or part of the public
with regard to its security (Germany-Austria video from March 2007);

(b) participating in the
transmission of demands from a group known as the Army of Islam, which took
hostages on March 12, 2007 in Gaza (kidnapping of journalist Alan Johnston);

(c)  inciting to participate in the
activities of insurgents (in Iraq, Afghanistan, and elsewhere), through the
distribution of material calling for a Jihad;

Compelling and/or using threats to
compel a government to do or refrain from doing an act and intimidating all or
a part of the public with regard to its security (Germany-Austria video from
March 2007);

[
22
]

The prosecution writes the following:

[
translation
]

2.2.1 The GIMF directly
participates in and counsels the commission of terrorist activities - Video
containing threats against Germany and Austria

On March 10, 2007, the GIMF made
the video public. The evidence respecting this video demonstrates that, on
March 7, 2007, Mohammed Mahmoud asked for this video to be uploaded and for
direct links to be created to view it. Saïd Namouh responded to this request
the same day and published several links to view it in different formats.

[
23
]

It is useful to reproduce the content of this
video, filed as Exhibit P-49:

[
translation
]

A letter to the governments of
Germany and Austria

In the name of God, Most Gracious,
Most Merciful.

Peace be upon him who follows the
straight path (straight path)

The voice of the Message greets you
and presents you with a letter to the governments of Germany and Austria, and
we say that the intelligent cannot destroy themselves and that the leaders of
people must serve the interests of their people before their own and those of
their allies.

(Photo of an armoured vehicle with
the German flag)

We wonder, what is the interest of
Germany in enlisting 2750 soldiers with NATO to fight, to defend the lies of
Bush and his cronies. The government has made an unlimited undertaking to
defend Bush and his cronies.  The German government lied to its people when it
declared

(Photos of Angela Merkel and
several German officials)

that the participation of German
soldiers in NATO forces is for peacekeeping and reconstruction.  It was their
big lie when they declared that they were sending their soldiers to Afghanistan
to avoid terrorist attacks in Germany.  Their first lie was that their soldiers
would take part in security and reconstruction and this is a lie and the world
believed it so it is true.  German newspapers published

(Photos of a newspaper, a soldier,
and skulls)

photos of their soldiers, how they
act as peacekeepers; the whole world saw the photos of their soldiers with the
skulls and skeletons of the dead.

Their second lie was that they were
sending their soldiers to Afghanistan to prevent terrorist attacks in their
country, but our Sheik Ayman el-Zawahiri had previously answered when he said:

(Photo of Sheik Ayman el-Zawahiri
making his statement)

Peace is a reciprocal matter. If we
are safe, you will be safe. If we are at peace, you will be at peace and if we
are going to be killed, God willing, you will be beaten and killed. That is the
exact equation. Try, then, to understand it if you understand.

(The photo of the hooded person
reappears, and he continues his statement)

Therefore,
Germany’s participation
with the United States of America against Islam and Muslims leads only to an
increase in threats against Germany and puts it in danger on its own territory

The situation must therefore be considered in context, and the same fate awaits
all those who ally themselves with them.

The presence of German forces in
Bakhshan (sp) and Khaldoun (sp) in the north of Afghanistan will not create
safety against attacks by the Mujahideen and the Taliban.  And Mullah Dadu
Allah declared some time ago that the actions of the Taliban will extend to
cover the north of Afghanistan.

(Photo of a thermal power plant and
another showing the logos of BMW, Mercedes, and Volkswagen)

O German government, Germany is
a state with a powerful economy and, until a not so distant past, a safe
state.  Why do you throw it all away for Bush and his cronies?

(Photos of Adidas ...   cellular
phone)

Would it not be idiotic to risk
this prosperous economy that exerts its influence throughout the world and
expose it to threat.  Would it not be idiotic to incite the Mujahideen to
commit attacks in your very home?

Your decision to side with the
Americans and your unlimited support of them has incited those you call
terrorists to consider you to be targets
and in
this way, you have destroyed your houses yourselves.

This is my advice to you;
withdraw your soldiers from Muslim countries and stop supporting Bush and his
cronies, it will be safer for you and your interests.

02:46

(Photo of the Austrian flag
....then police officers wearing protective helmets)

And to Austria, we say:

Your soldiers in Afghanistan do not
represent an exact (image) or direct threat to our Mujahideen brothers.

(Photos of soldiers)

but they represent a real support
for Bush and his cronies. The truth that the Austrian government wanted for its
people is for these soldiers to operate with NATO even though you are a neutral
country and are not part of NATO.  How can a neutral country participate in the
military force of an alliance without being a member? And where is its
neutrality by siding with the Americans and their support against Muslims?
(Photo of a resort … swimmers   ...

Austria was one of the safest
countries in the world, its people were in no real threat, its economy was
flourishing. It (Austria) relies primarily on summer and winter tourism, which
brings in huge amounts of money every year.

(Photo of the Austrian flag)

However, in the event of some
kind of threat to safety, Austria would be on the list of countries targeted by
the mujahideen and that state would change.

(Photo of  - poss. - ministers)

We speak to the new socialist
ministers’ council that promised its people the justice, lawfulness,
prosperity, and security of withdrawing its soldiers from Afghanistan, of
stopping their support for Bush’s war against Muslims.  Austria has no real
interest in all of this.

Therefore, do not demolish an
entire country for five soldiers that you have sent to Afghanistan.  We also
warn you that soldiers are close to the Mujahideen and they are closer than the
others.  At the moment, the Mujahideen are preparing for springtime attacks and
the world fears them before they even happen.  Settle your affairs (actions) as
quickly as possible and withdraw your soldiers; this war is not yours and you
do not have the capacity for it.  This war is between the Mujahideen and
America and all of those who stand beside it (America).

Withdraw from its ranks. The
intelligent do not destroy their own security with their own hands, they
reinforce their economy instead of weakening it. The amounts that you spend on
Bush and his cronies, you could spend on the scholars, whom you have failed in
your promises.  The socialist party led by the current government alliance
should prove its sincerity for peace and security and may it not do as the
socialist party did in Spain that betrayed its people; it withdrew its soldiers
from Iraq and sent 600 others to Afghanistan.  In reality, it did nothing.

Muslim countries in effect
represent a single country. By sending its soldiers to Afghanistan, it (the
Spanish government) put its country under threat once again.

Live up to your responsibility,
make the right decision, and do not miss the opportunity, only to regret it one
day when regrets will be futile.

Et à la fin de notre message, Nous
remercions Dieu de l’univers.

[
24
]

The message to Austria and Germany clearly
constitutes a threat of terrorist activity within the meaning of s. 83.01 and
is itself terrorist activity.

The GIMF facilitates, participates
directly in, and counsels the commission of terrorist activities - logistical
support during the taking of Alan Johnston as hostage

[
25
]

The prosecution writes:

[translation]

2.2.2 The GIMF facilitates,
participates directly in, and counsels the commission   Johnston

The Court must now turn to the second stage of
analysis under
Carter
and determine the participation of the accused in
the conspiracy.

Second
stage pursuant to
Carter
: Is the accused part of this conspiracy?

[
139
]

This question is analyzed on the basis of a
balance of probabilities. Only evidence directly admissible against the accused
may be considered. This evidence must be considered in context, however. In
Canadian Criminal Evidence,
McWilliam states the following
concerning the second stage under
Carter
:

At this stage, the trier of fact is
not required to view the accused's conduct or utterances in isolation or
divorced from the context in which they occurred. Rather, the trier of
fact is entitled to view the accused's own acts and declarations against the
picture provided by the acts and declarations of the co-conspirators. At the
end of the day, however, the assessment of probable membership in the relevant
criminal venture must be made on the basis of evidence admissible against the
individual accused.

[
140
]

Thus, the words of the accused in the thirty-one
conversations must not be analyzed in isolation while ignoring the words of the
others with whom he was interacting. The words of the others can be used to
understand the meaning of those of the accused.

[
141
]

In addition, the words of the others may
constitute an exception to the hearsay rule, in that they were uttered in the
presence of the accused who, through his attitude and replies, adopted the
content of what they said. In this way, they are admissible against the accused
in the second stage pursuant to
Carter
.

[
142
]

This is the case in the thirty-one conversations
already referred to in this respect.

[
143
]

The personal involvement of the accused in the
conversations analyzed demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the
accused participated in the conspiracy.

[
144
]

The Court must now consider whether the evidence
as a whole demonstrates beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty of
this charge.

Third stage pursuant to
Carter
:
Does the evidence as a whole demonstrate his guilt beyond all reasonable doubt?
